**Video:** [Lec 08 — Distribution Estimation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aYb8KG9JYsg)

### Learning goals
- Restate the raw material of ML: an i.i.d. dataset from unknown $P_{X,Y}$
- List what we might estimate: joints, marginals, conditionals, or moments
- Map real questions (disease rate, diagnose image, …) to the right $P$
- Understand supervised / unsupervised as naming conventions, not different physics

### Before this clicks
Lectures 6–7: data points live in ranges of RVs; $\mathcal{D}$ is modeled as i.i.d. samples from an unknown law. Independence = product of joints; identical = same law for each sample.

---

## 1. Starting point

$$
\mathcal{D}=\bigl\{(x_i,y_i)\bigr\}_{i=1}^{n}
\sim_{\text{i.i.d.}} P_{X,Y}\ \text{(unknown)}.
$$

- $x_i\in\mathbb{R}^{D}$ — features / inputs / “data”
- $y_i\in\mathbb{R}^{K}$ or discrete categories — outputs / “labels” (optional)

Both $X$ and $Y$ are RVs on one $\Omega$. Labels may be absent; then we only have $\{x_i\}$.

**Data is the raw material** — algorithms are only as good as the samples they see.

---

## 2. Foundational problem

$$
\text{Given }\mathcal{D}\text{ from unknown }P,\quad
\text{estimate }P,\quad\text{and/or learn to sample from }P.
$$

| Focus | Common name |
|-------|-------------|
| Estimate useful laws / conditionals; sampling secondary | Discriminative methods |
| Emphasize generating new samples | Generative methods |

This course leans on **estimation**; a later course goes deep on generative sampling.

Sometimes we do not need the full law — only a **moment** (expectation, second moment, …). That is still “learning about $P$.”

---

## 3. Which distribution? Depends on the question

Fix a dataset of images with disease labels. Different questions pick different targets:

| Real question | Target |
|---------------|--------|
| Given this image, how likely is disease? | $P(Y\mid X)$ |
| How common is disease in the population (ignore pixels)? | $P_{Y}$ |
| How do pixels look in general (ignore labels)? | $P_{X}$ |
| How do pixels look **among diseased cases**? | $P(X\mid Y=y)$ |
| Full coupled story of image and label | $P_{X,Y}$ |

**Classification / regression** (conventional names): estimate $P(Y\mid X)$.

- discrete $Y$ $\to$ classification  
- continuous $Y\in\mathbb{R}^{K}$ $\to$ regression  

Boundaries are thin; inpainting can be “$P(Y\mid X)$” where $Y$ is just masked pixels of $X$.

---

## 4. Conditioning reminder

When we write $P(X\mid Y)$ or $p(x\mid y)$:

- the **conditioned** variable is fixed to a value,
- the object is a distribution **over the other** variable,
- changing the fixed value changes the conditional law.

So conditionals are functions of the conditioning value.

---

## 5. Supervised vs unsupervised (know the words)

| Conventional phrase | Meaning in industry talk |
|---------------------|---------------------------|
| Supervised | Labels present; used in the algorithm |
| Unsupervised | No labels |

Mathematically in this course: labels are just another RV / dimensions. Human labeling is costly — that is why “supervised” feels expensive — but the abstract problem is still distribution estimation.

Self-supervised learning: carve fake labels out of $X$ itself.

---

## 6. Preview: densities next

Class mostly writes **density** functions (for continuous RVs) for algorithmic convenience, while conceptually we still mean the underlying **distribution / measure**. Lecture 9 makes that precise.

---

## 7. Tiny concrete example

$n=10{,}000$ chest X-rays, $y_i\in\{0,1\}$.

1. Screen a new scan $\to$ need $\widehat{P}(Y\mid X=x_{\text{new}})$.  
2. Report prevalence $\to$ need $\widehat{P}(Y=1)$ (can ignore images).  
3. Build a “disease look” synthesizer $\to$ need something like $\widehat{P}(X\mid Y=1)$ plus a sampler.

Same $\mathcal{D}$; three different estimation targets.

---

## 8. Common confusions

| Confusion | Clarification |
|-----------|----------------|
| $P_Y$ vs $P(X\mid Y)$ | $P_Y$ never looks at pixels; $P(X\mid Y)$ is the law of images for a fixed label. |
| Estimating $P_{X,Y}$ always means generative sampling | You can estimate a joint without shipping a sampler. |
| One true supervised/unsupervised split in math | Naming; both are distribution estimation. |
| IID is an English vibe | It is a precise product / same-law assumption used by algorithms. |
